question: A 5-year-old boy has generalised oedema, urine protein 3+ on dipstick, serum albumin 16 g/L, and normal BP. Urine microscopy shows no casts or haematuria. Which category of proteinuria does this best represent?

answers.text: Tubular proteinuria due to proximal tubular dysfunction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tubular proteinuria involves low-molecular-weight proteins (beta-2 microglobulin) and does not cause heavy proteinuria or hypoalbuminaemia of this degree.

answers.text: Overflow proteinuria due to excessive plasma protein production

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Overflow proteinuria (e.g., Bence-Jones protein in myeloma) is extremely rare in children; it requires a source of excess abnormal protein exceeding tubular reabsorption capacity.

Correct. Heavy proteinuria (>40 mg/m²/hr), hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L), generalised oedema, and absence of haematuria/hypertension are the hallmarks of nephrotic syndrome, caused by glomerular barrier dysfunction.
Orthostatic proteinuria is benign, present only in the upright position, and does not cause hypoalbuminaemia or oedema.

overallFeedback.feedback: The triad of heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L), and oedema defines nephrotic syndrome — a manifestation of glomerular barrier failure (charge and size selectivity lost).
This is classic nephrotic syndrome — heavy glomerular proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and no haematuria or hypertension.
